Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
DETAILED ACTION
This office action is responsive to application filed on 09/15/2021. In the application,
Claims 1-5 and 10-19 are pending and being considered.
Claims 1, 10 and 15 are independent.
Claims 6-9 have been cancelled.
Claims 5, 14 and 19 are objected.
Claims 1-4, 10-13 and 15-18 are rejected.
Foreign Priority
This application is a National Stage of International Application No. PCT/CN2020/079104, filed on March 13, 2020, which claims priority to Chinese Patent Application No. 201910220920.7, filed on March 22, 2019. Both of the aforementioned applications are hereby incorporated by reference in their entireties.
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 09/15/2021 and 04/18/2022 are filed on or after the mailing date of the application no.17/439,467 filed on 09/15/2021. The submission is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97.  Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner and an initialed and dated copy of Applicant’s IDS form 1449 filed on 09/15/2021 and 04/18/2022 is attached to the instant office action.
Abstract
Applicant is reminded of the proper language and format for an abstract of the disclosure.
The abstract should be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph on a separate sheet within the range of 50 to 150 words in length. The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether there is a need for consulting the full patent text for details.
The language should be clear and concise and should not repeat information given in the title. It should avoid using phrases which can be implied, such as, “The disclosure concerns,” “The disclosure defined by this invention,” “The disclosure describes,” etc. In addition, the form and legal phraseology often used in patent claims, such as “means” and “said,” should be avoided.
The abstract of the disclosure is objected to because it repeats information given in the title, such as “file access right authentication method and electronic device”. Examiner respectfully suggests applicant to amend the Abstract language and re-write it in a clear and concise manner by avoiding the information given in the title. Correction is required.  See MPEP § 608.01(b).
Specification
1.	The use of the term “Bluetooth”, which is a trade name or a mark used in commerce, has been noted in this application. The term should be accompanied by the generic terminology; furthermore the term should be capitalized wherever it appears or, where appropriate, include a proper symbol indicating use in commerce such as ™, SM , or ® following the term.
Although the use of trade names and marks used in commerce (i.e., trademarks, service marks, certification marks, and collective marks) are permissible in patent applications, the proprietary nature of the marks should be respected and every effort made to prevent their use in any manner which might adversely affect their validity as commercial marks.
2.	The lengthy specification has not been checked to the extent necessary to determine the presence of all possible minor errors. Applicant’s cooperation is requested in correcting any errors of which applicant may become aware in the specification.
Claim Objections
Claims 1-5, 11-14 and 16-19 are objected due to the following informalities:
Regarding independent claim 1, the claim recites contingent (conditional) limitations “determining if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, and determining that authentication of the file access request succeeds if the first fixed identify information matches the authorized fixed identity information” that contains “if” statement(s), as optional (conditional) language. Language that suggests or makes optional (conditional) but does not require steps to be performed or does not limit a claim to a particular structure does not limit the scope of a claim or claim limitation. According to MPEP (§ 2111.04, subsection II), “the broadest reasonable interpretation of a method (or process) claim having contingent limitations requires only those steps that must be performed and does not include steps that are not required to be performed because the condition(s) precedent are not met”. For example, when analyzing the claimed method as a whole, if the condition for performing a contingent step is not satisfied, the performance recited by the step need not be carried out in order for the claimed method to be performed […]. Therefore [t]he Examiner did not need to present evidence of the obviousness of the method steps of claim 1 that are not required to be performed under a broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim” (See Ex parte Schulhauser, Appeal 2013-007847 (PTAB April 28, 2016) for an analysis of contingent claim limitations in the context of both method claims and system claims). For examination purpose, and in view of the Fig. 5 (steps 503-505) and associated paragraph [0091-00102], under BRI, examiner interprets that the claim limitations as recited are directed to the step of ‘determining’ that authentication of the file access request succeeds only if the first fixed identify information matches the authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, and authentication of the file access request fails if the first fixed identify information does not match with the authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file. Therefore, examiner did not need to present evidence of the obviousness of the method step of “determining that authentication of the file access request succeeds”, under BRI of the claim, if the first fixed identify information does not match with the authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file (See Ex parte Schulhauser, Appeal 2013-007847 (PTAB April 28, 2016) as disclosed above). Applicant is suggested to make appropriate corrections in light of the immediate specification to overcome this objection.
Regrading claim 2, the claim is objected for the same reasons as mentioned above for the independent claim 1, since the claim 2 also recites similar contingent (conditional) limitations. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claims 2, 11 and 16, the claims recite “if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file”, which should be corrected and rewritten as “if the first fixed identity information matches the authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file”, since the term “authorized fixed identity information” has already been recited in the independent claims 1, 10 and 16 upon which claims 2, 11 and 16 are dependent, respectively. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claims 2, 11 and 16, the claims further recite “if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, decrypt file-key ciphertext by using the first fixed identity information, and when the decryption succeeds, …”, in which term “the decryption” lacks antecedent basis. For examination purpose, and in view of the Fig. 5 (steps 505-506) and associated paragraph [00102-00105], examiner interprets that the recited term “the decryption” refers to decrypt a file-key ciphertext by using the first fixed identity information if the first fixed identity information matches the authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file. Applicant is suggested to make appropriate correction by amending the limitation in a clear and concise manner to overcome this objection.
Regarding claims 3, 12 and 17, the claims are objected for the same reasons for reciting “the decryption” as mentioned above for claims 2, 11 and 16, respectively. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claims 4 and 5, the claims recite “wherein before the receiving, by the electronic device, a file access request, the method further comprises”, which should be corrected and rewritten as “wherein, before the file access request, the method further comprises”, since the limitation “receiving a file access request” has already been recited in the independent claim 1 upon which claims 4 and 5 are dependent. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claim 5, the claim further recites “the matching, by the electronic device, the first fixed identity information with authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file comprises:” which lacks antecedent basis for “the matching”. For examination purpose, and in view of the Fig. 5 (steps 503-505) and associated paragraph [0098-0102], examiner interprets that the recited “the matching, by the electronic device, the first fixed identity information with authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file comprises:” refers to the step of “determining if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file”, as recited in the independent claim 1. Therefore, applicant is suggested to rewrite the claim limitation(s) in a clear and concise manner. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claims 13 and 14, the claims are objected for the same reasons as mentioned above for claims 4 and 5, respectively, Therefore, appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claims 18 and 19, the claims are objected for the same reasons as mentioned above for claims 4 and 5, respectively, Therefore, appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 5, 14 and 19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA  the applicant regards as the invention.
Regarding claim 5, the claim recites limitation the matching”, which has not been defined previously. Therefore, there is insufficient antecedent basis for “the matching” in the claim. Applicant is suggested to clarify with correct antecedent basis for “the matching”, as described above in the claim objection for claim 5.
Regarding claims 14 and 19, the claims are rejected for the same reasons as mentioned above for claim 5. Appropriate correction is required.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 5, 14 and 19 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected claim, but would be allowable only if rewritten in independent form for including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims, and amended to overcome the claim objections and rejections under 112(b), as described above.
Claim Rejections - 35 U.S.C. 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or non-obviousness.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1, 10 and 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Umebayashi et al. (US 20040010701 A1; hereinafter “Ume”) in view of Yang et al. (US 2018/0102902 A1; hereinafter “Yang”).
Regarding independent claim 1, Ume teaches A file access right authentication method for an electronic device, the method comprising (Ume, Para. [0014], discloses a data protection method for effectively preventing unauthorized access to a resource storage that stores data files (see Fig. 3), and as disclosed in Fig. 2 and Para. [0052], wherein a computer 100 can be used to implement the method embodiment of the present invention):
receiving a file access request, wherein the file access request includes Ume, Para. [0080], discloses that the application 230 outputs an access request for the file 111a in the folder 111 in step S12. The access request may comprise a request to generate the file 111a, a request to refer to the file 111a (e.g., read a file), a request to update the file 111a, and a request to delete the file 111a. The access request which is outputted from the application 230 is transferred to a driver 240);
obtaining the first process identifier and determining first fixed identity information corresponding to the first process identifier (Ume, Para. [0081], discloses that the driver 240 acquires the process ID of the application 230 in response to the access request which is outputted from the application 230. The driver 240 refers to the access permission management table 210, and retrieves therefrom a client identifier corresponding to the acquired process ID, and as disclosed in Fig. 4 and Para. [0071-0072], an access permission management table 210 that has a column of client identifiers contains identification information (client identifiers; e.g., first fixed identity information) of processing functions such as the application 230 executed as a client.); and
determining if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, and determining that authentication of the file access request succeeds if the first fixed identity information matches the authorized fixed identity information (Ume, Para. [0068 and/or 0112], discloses that after the identification information about the application 230 which has outputted the file access request for the file has been acquired by the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243, then the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243 determines whether the file access request for the resource to be protected is to be permitted or not. Specifically, if information matching a combination of the identification information about the application and the folder (in which the file to be accessed) of the access destination is registered in the access permission management table 210, then the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243 permits accessing the file. Or see also Fig. 13 and Para. [0109], that shows a process of accessing a file. The application 230 outputs a file access request in step S81. The file access request is received by the driver 240. The driver 240 refers to the protection resource management table 220, and confirms whether the file to be accessed in response to the file access request is a file in the folder to be monitored or not in step S82. If the file to be accessed is a file in the folder to be monitored, then the driver 240 refers to the access permission management table 210 (e.g., by verifying client ID/identification information) and confirms whether access to the file by the application 230 which has outputted the file access request is permitted or not in step S83. If access to the file by the application 230 is permitted, then the driver 240 accesses the file in response to the file access request, and returns the result to the application 230 in step S84.).
Ume, as described above, teaches to ‘obtaining the first process identifier and determining first fixed identity information corresponding to the first process identifier’, however Ume fails to explicitly disclose but Yang teaches wherein the file access request includes a first process identifier (Yang, Para. [0145], discloses that, at 302, a read request is received from a requesting process P having a corresponding process ID. The read request also includes file identifying information enabling the data protection module to identify the data file F being requested (e.g., by identifying the file path of the data file), or see also Para. [0173], discloses that the request may include a process ID P, file identifying information for a file F…).
Thus, it would have been obvious to one ordinary skilled in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to have modified ‘Ume’ by incorporating ‘wherein the file access request includes a first process identifier’, as taught by Yang, in order to manage data access of processes executing on a computer system and protects data from data breaches and known or unknown attacks including ransomware and/or phishing attacks; Yang, Abstract and Para. [0002].
Regrading independent Claim 10, the claim has limitations similar to those treated in the above rejection(s) for the independent claim 1, and are met by the references as discussed above. Independent claim 10, however, also recites the following limitations “An electronic device, comprising a memory, a processor, and a computer program that is stored in the memory and that, when executed by the processor, causes the computer device to:”, which is disclosed in Fig. 2 and Para. [0052-0053] of the cited prior art ‘Ume’.
Regrading independent Claim 15, the claim has limitations similar to those treated in the above rejection(s) for the independent claim 1, and are met by the references as discussed above. Independent claim 15, however, also recites the following limitations “A non-transitory computer readable medium, wherein the computer readable storage medium comprises a computer program that, when executed by a processor of an electronic device, cause the electronic device to:”, which is disclosed in claim 10 and Para. [0150-0153] of the cited prior art ‘Ume’.
Claims 2-3, 11-12 and 16-17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Umebayashi et al. (US 20040010701 A1; hereinafter “Ume”) in view of Yang et al. (US 2018/0102902 A1; hereinafter “Yang”), and further in view of Ohmori et al. (US 2008/0235517 A1; hereinafter “Ohmori”) and Asano, Tomoyuki (US 2003/0142826 A1; hereinafter “Asano”).
Regarding claim 2, Ume as modified by Yang teaches the method according to claim 1, wherein Ume further teaches the determining that authentication of the file access request succeeds comprises: if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, decrypting file-key ciphertext Ume, Para. [0068-0069 & 0083], discloses that the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243 determines whether the file access request for the resource to be protected is to be permitted or not. Specifically, if information matching a combination of the identification information about the application and the folder (in which the file to be accessed) of the access destination is registered in the access permission management table 210, then the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243 permits accessing the file. If the access permission/inhibition determining unit 243 permits a file access request for the resource to be protected, then the encryption/decryption processor 244 encrypts or decrypts the file specified by the file access request. Specifically, if the file access request is a file reference request, then the encryption/decryption processor 244 extracts the specified file from the folder to be protected, and decrypts the file into plaintext data (e.g., file-key ciphertext)), and
when the decryption succeeds, determining that the authentication of the file access request succeeds, wherein Ume, Para. [0118 and 0119], discloses that the encryption/decryption processor 244 carries out a file accessing process including file encryption or decryption on the file to be accessed, using the acquired key. Specifically, if the file access request is a request to read the file, then the encryption/decryption processor 244 decrypts the file to be accessed with the acquired key, and transfers the decrypted file to the application 230. If the file access request is a request to write the file, then the encryption/decryption processor 244 encrypts the data to be written with the acquired key, forms a file thereof, and stores the file in the folder to be monitored).
Ume, as described above, teaches ‘wherein the determining that authentication of the file access request succeeds comprises: if the first fixed identity information matches authorized fixed identity information corresponding to the first file, decrypting file-key ciphertext, and wherein a file key is used to encrypt the first file’, however the combination of ‘Ume as modified by Yang’ fails to explicitly disclose but Ohmori teaches decrypting file-key ciphertext by using the first fixed identity information (Ohmori, Para. [0026], discloses that the encryption processing unit uses the encryption scheme indicated by the identification information only for decrypting a ciphertext, and as disclosed in Para. [0199], wherein the encryption scheme indicated by the identification information may include a program file name (e.g., program package name, as indicated in paragraph 0033 of the immediate specification)), and
Thus, it would have been obvious to one ordinary skilled in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to have modified the combination of ‘Ume as modified by Yang’ by incorporating ‘decrypting file-key ciphertext by using the first fixed identity information’, as taught by Ohmori, such modification would provide an enhanced decryption scheme that would prevent use of unauthorized file contents obtained by tampering and eavesdropping; Ohmori, Para. [0002].
Ume as modified by Yang in view of Ohmori fails to explicitly disclose but Asano teaches wherein the file-key ciphertext is ciphertext of a file key (Asano, Para. [0081], discloses that the decrypted key ciphertext provides the receiver with the content key (e.g., as cleartext). The receiver can then access the content file in the clear by decrypting the encrypted content file using the content key).
Thus, it would have been obvious to one ordinary skilled in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to have modified the combination of ‘Ume as modified by Yang in view of Ohmori’ by incorporating ‘wherein the file-key ciphertext is ciphertext of a file key’, as taught by Asano, such modification would provide access for authorized receivers to the content of encrypted content file while preventing revoked receivers (i.e., unauthorized receivers) from accessing the encrypted content of file; Asano, Para. [0042].
Regarding claim 3, Ume as modified by Yang in view of Ohmori and Asano teaches the method according to claim 2, wherein Ume further teaches the method further comprises: when the decryption fails, determining that the authentication of the file access request fails (Ume, Para. [0050], discloses that a file or other data which is stored in the resource 1 by a certain application is encrypted using a key that is generated by the application. Therefore, an attempt to access a file stored in the resource 1 from an application that is not legitimately activated fails to decrypt the file. As a result, it is possible to prevent and monitor the unauthorized processing and leakage of information based on an operation according to a program that is not permitted to access the resource 1. Stated otherwise, a legitimate user who is permitted to access information of the file is inhibited from unauthorized control of the resource 1 through an unauthorized operation via a program that is not desired by the system administrator.).
Regarding claims 11-12, the claims are drawn to the electronic device and have limitations similar to the method claims 2-3, respectively. Therefore, the claims 11-12 are rejected for the same reasons of anticipation (obviousness) as used above for the method claims 2-3, respectively.
Regarding claim 16-17, the claims are drawn to the non-transitory computer readable medium and have limitations similar to the method claims 2-3, respectively. Therefore, the claims 16-17 are rejected for the same reasons of anticipation (obviousness) as used above for the method claims 2-3, respectively.
Claims 4, 13 and 18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Umebayashi et al. (US 20040010701 A1; hereinafter “Ume”) in view of Yang et al. (US 2018/0102902 A1; hereinafter “Yang”), and further in view of Robert Scott Chapman, III (US 2016/0196442 A1; hereinafter “Chapman”).
Regarding claim 4, Ume as modified by Yang teaches the method according to claim 1, wherein Ume further teaches before the receiving, by the electronic device, a file access request, the method further comprises (Ume, Fig. 1 and Para. [0038 & 0040], discloses that first, identification information 2a about a program which can access the resource 1 is registered in an access permission management table 3 (step S1 in Fig. 1). In the example shown in FIG. 1, program A is registered as identification information 2a about a program which can access the resource 1 […]. Thereafter, when an access request 2c for accessing to the resource 1 is received, identification information 4 about the request source program 2 which has outputted the access request 2c is acquired (step S2 in Fig. 1)):
obtaining a process identifier and fixed identity information of a running application program (Ume, Fig. 1 and Para. [0038], discloses that, at step S1 in Fig. 1, identification information 2a about a program which can access the resource 1 is registered in an access permission management table 3. In the example shown in FIG. 1, program A is registered as identification information 2a about a program which can access the resource 1 […], and as disclosed in Para. [0091], the application 230 outputs a registration request to register the process ID which is allocated when the process is activated),
however, the combination of ‘Ume as modified by Yang’ fails to explicitly disclose but Chapman teaches establishing a correspondence between the process identifier and the fixed identity information (Chapman, Fig. 7 and Para. [0088], discloses a data structure 700 that is configured to store zero or more records 710. In this example, each record includes fields for a process ID, a user ID, an application, a path, and a file name. The process ID is the process ID assigned to an instance of an executing software application by the OS. The “application” field is the name of the application associated with the process ID. The “file name” field is the name of the document being accessed by the corresponding process ID. (herein, name of application and/or file name represents fixed identity information)), and establishing a correspondence between a newly created file and the fixed identity information (Chapman, Para. [0085 and 0088], discloses that if the monitoring software 342 does not find a record in its data structure for the command’s process ID, the monitoring software 342 generates a new record for its data structure (as depicted in Fig. 7) and stores information associated with the command, such as the process ID, user ID, name of application, path name and file name of the accessed file. For example, and as depicted in Fig. 7, where a process ID “12” is associated with an application name “FileSync” corresponding to a file name “finance2013.xlsx”).
Thus, it would have been obvious to one ordinary skilled in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to have modified the combination of ‘Ume as modified by Yang’ by incorporating ‘establishing a correspondence between the process identifier and the fixed identity information; and establishing a correspondence between a newly created file and the fixed identity information’, as taught by Chapman, in order to establish a data structure for tracking processes (process IDs) that attempt to perform commands on the secure data and secures data by determining whether a command in the command queue should be allowed or not; Chapman, Para. [0084 and 0088].
Regarding claim 13, the claim is drawn to the electronic device and have limitations similar to the method claim 4. Therefore, the claim 13 is rejected for the same reasons of anticipation (obviousness) as used above for the method claim 4.
Regarding claim 18, the claim is drawn to the non-transitory computer readable medium and have limitations similar to the method claim 4. Therefore, the claim 18 is rejected for the same reasons of anticipation (obviousness) as used above for the method claim 4.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.
1.	Chambliss et al. (US 20170093844 A1) is directed to access control of data, and more particularly to regulation of access by an access program to a data object residing in a storage system.
2.	Nakamura et al. (US 20150363189 A1) discloses to monitor processes generated by an installer for the software when the software is installed. The operation unit generates, based on file information about files accessed by the generated processes and the relationships between the processes, software configuration information associating the file information about the files with the software.
3.	Sasaki et al. (US 5870477 A) discloses that when the IDs's coincide with each other, so that it is judged that decryption is possible. Such as, the ciphertext data is deciphered using the deciphered management key (step 348), and plaintext data obtained by the decryption is displayed on the display unit 2.
4.	Sun, Zhe (CN 108228770 A) discloses to determine the application package name corresponding to the id of the corresponding relation of the process name and the determination of the target file corresponding to the application package name.
